The Elder Scrolls:

I started playing the games with Daggerfall, in 1995. Exactly what I loved about the game was the incredible detail and complexity - the near endless roleplaying possibilities. And that's the exact part of the game that Beth has systematically removed and replaced with shiny graphics and shallow gimmicks. I actually gave up on the series after Oblivion. I refused to buy Skyrim, and have never regretted that decision.

Need for Speed:

Shift was the last one I bought, and I hated it. The NFS series has generally had a tendency toward arcade style instead of simulation style (with the exception of the tremendous Porsche Unleashed), but even with the worst of their arcade-ish games, they made a stab at some realism, and generally managed to pull it off. And if nothing else, the games were generally fun (particularly Underground 2 and Carbon). I really had hopes for the series after ProStreet, which has some gameplay flaws (lack of support for digital controllers being far and away the most significant) but had pretty impressive physics for an NFS game. But then they put out the godawful Shift.

I have no idea what the hell they were thinking. They spent a pile of money on an entirely new physics engine, and had far and away the most accurate and believable suspension and traction simulation they'd ever had, and then they completely destroyed it by having all of the cars pivot around the driver's seat like slot cars, just to accommodate the cockpit view gimmick. What sort of idiots model physics as accurately as possible, then deliberately destroy what they've so painstakingly modeled? I haven't even kept track of what they've done after that.

Out of curiosity, are there any specific things about recent Zeldas you dislike?

A few tropes that have come up since the originals but have become mostly standard:

  1. The weapon/item you get in a dungeon is the key to finishing it and/or defeating the boss. I don't hate this, but to feels more authentic for the dungeon being a place I have to conquer for the MacGuffin (piece of triforce, 7 maidens, etc), instead of an elaborate temple devoted to the item that sits inside. Fixing this would improve Zelda micro/mid gameplay the most, because it encourages me to experiment.

  2. Massive, massive artificial gating and backtracking. Ocarina is filled with these. Can't proceed to place B because you're blocked by person X and you have to talk to person Y. I like Zelda games that let me explore and even allow me to get into perilous situations of my own making. I'm going to include sidequests here. Neat things to do on the side is cool, but in a lot of games I'm required to participate in them to progress the storyline. Zelda's macro gameplay as a result just isn't fun to me. Metroid seems to do this much much better with lots of toys and generally being massively stronger the second time through an area versus the first, while Zelda kind of progressively makes me retread only slightly more powerful.*

  3. The "fanboy" lore. It's not enough that Zelda is a game, it has to have a bunch of story that fits with fan expectations, the presumptuous insistence on timelines and lineage. The lore that popped up around Zelda reminds me a little of Sonic's lore. At least Zelda fans aren't insufferable like many Sonic extended universe fans. I like to discover an individual game's universe on my own. I'm not saying it needs to be as stark as the original Zelda which had no in-game lore, but even Final Fantasy -- massively scripted and scenario driven -- leaves me at least a little wiggle room in interpretation.

*Edit: I recently played through Shantae Risky's Revenge and I loved the fact that as you got stronger, they mixed up the enemies and made them stronger in the paths you had to retread, let's me play with my power ups and still prevents things from being a cakewalk. I think that's a good example that backtracking doesn't always mean that you have to leave a massacre the next time through.
